You won't get along without defining data tables as such. Don't know
how well the disassembler is at this- some disassemblers even figure
out data vs. code areas themselves... but i don't know which do/don't.

Your problem is: l0834 and l0836 are the location of the second byte

so that's easy. But to have a lable at $0836, you'd need to break the
opcode up:

l0835 .byte xx
l0836 .byte yy

or write something like:

l0835 jr l0856
l0836 .equ l0835+1

I have no clue why this is not done, but most disassemblers choke on
jumps to the argument of an instruction. On the 6502 processor, this
is even used quite frequently in 'real' code, like this:

print_a: lda #'a'
 .by $2c 
print_b: lda #'b'
 jmp print_out

($2c is a compare instruction and takes a two byte operand. If you do
a print_a, only the flags are set, but the lda #'b' is not executed.)

Even there, almost all 6502 disassemblers will head straightforward
and neither list the lda #'b' nor assign the print_b label. Think of
the algorythm being 'is this address jumped to? If yes then insert a
label' and not (what you would like) 'i have a jump instruction;
insert a label there'

> I guess what surprises me is that the writers of the
> disassemblers (two have done this so far) didn't think
> that this would ever be an issue.

As i said: even if they should, they won't...

> In many cases there 
> is no way to know what is data in a binary file, and
> there are bound to be lots of cases where labels will
> point in the middle of an opcode until it can be gone 
> through by hand.

Another thing automatic disassemblies can suffer from: 'offset
errors'. Imagine the last data byte is a CD (Z80: call nnnn), the
first instruction of the 'real' code gets hidden in the argument of
the call instruction. This effect can propagate for many lines of code.

> By not putting in all these labels,
> it creates a file that, in my case at least, has way 
> too many errors to correct by hand. 

Correctly re-assembling the generated listing is only a small step-
you could achieve this by converting everything to .byte
'instructions', to use the other extreme.

Out of interest: Do the arcade ROMs use 'clean' code, with large
chunks of code and data, or does every second subroutine have it's own
data table? Or do they have the mechanism that's used with the home
console: Define 'call xxxx: .word mmmm: .byte nn' as a subroutine that
takes 'inline' parameters ('mmmm' and 'nn') and returns to the byte
after that? If so, you would end up with really many data area
defines- and better program that special case into the disassembler.
The Amstrad CPC fans have done so, as they have the same problem (the
RST instructions generally expect a word parameter, making them into
modified jump and call instructions)

Another, even more nasty tweak: an arbitrary subroutine call with an
inline parameter of varying length. I'll write it in Z80, but it was
implemented on the Commodore Plus/4 and 128:

 call print_inline_string
 .ascii 'Hello World!'
 .byte 0; end of string marker
 ld hl, init; normal code goes on

Hope something of this is helpful for someone...

Hello all, I am new to this newsgroup. I worked on the original 
Bally Arcade back in the 70's at Dave Nutting and Associates. It is 
nice to see all of the interest in our work from back then.

I don't know how much I remember, being that it was 25 years ago I 
last worked on the Bally Arcade, but I might be able to fill in a 
few details.

I noticed that TERSE was mentioned. TERSE is an acronym and it 
stands for Terse Efficient Recursive Stack Engine. And for you real 
observant types, yes the name itself is also recursive. I think it 
was Al McNeil (sp?) that did the original work on the engine itself 
and came up with the name. He was my office-mate at DNA for awhile 
before he went to Stern. All of TERSE was written in house. Once you 
disassemble the engine in Z80 code, pretty much everything else was 
written in TERSE so you would need a TERSE disassembler. 

I first started at DNA in 1977 and my first cartridge was 
SeaWolf/Missle and I remember developing that using the wire-wrapped 
boards before the chipset was back from the fabricators. I have fond 
memories of flexing those huge boards to get them to work! I also 
developed Panzer Attack/Red Barron, Grand Prix/Demo Derby, 
Blackjack/Poker/Acey Ducey -- I actually finished the development 
started by Mason, but he didn't shuffle the cards correctly. I used 
Donald Knuths shuffle algorithm which worked just great. I also co-
authored the Football cartridge with Bob Ogden when he first joined. 
He played football in college and I was a wiz at programming 
cartridges! The other work I did for them was all proto-types that 
never went to market. I think I wrote the proto-types in TERSE and 
the rest was straight Z80 code.

Hello and bye for now.

Rickey Spiece

Hello,

While we're on the subject of Forth and the Bally hardware...

I worked on the emulations of Bally chipset for the MAME and MESS emulators.  For a long while, no-one had managed to emulate Professor Pacman, and there was speculation that the rom images were corrupt.  At some point, I started to dig into the code, and to my surprise I discovered a Forth interpreter in there! :)  This explained why a lot of the code didn't disassemble, it was mostly Forth byte code.

Ironically, this actually helped me figure out the bank-switching in that game.  I disassembled some of the interpreter, and found the code for an "absolute jump".  By searching for this byte sequence, I managed to piece together where each ROM was switched into the memory map.  I still needed other techniques, but eventually it was emulated successfully.

Along the way, I looked a bit further and discovered that most of the Bally coin-ops were written this way.  I could even see the interpreter revisions from one coin-op to the next.  Jamie also confirmed to me that it was TERSE.

Thanks,
-Frank

P.S. Last month, I managed to add the "Demons and Dragons" prototype to that MAME driver as well.

I started looking at bugs in MESS related to the Astrocade.

Unfortunately, sound was completely broken by a change made between version
0.95 and 0.96, and I guess no one noticed.  I applied a fix and it should be
back in the next release version.

I looked at why ICBM Attack wouldn't start in the emulator.   Strangely,
this game uses the stack pointer before it initializes it.  On a cold start,
it uses a BIOS trap (RST 0x38) to call a function (0x19) to initialize the
color registers.  This requires the stack pointer to be pointing to RAM.
After that, it clears some memory and initializes the stack pointer.

So, ICBM Attack won't start in the latest MESS from a cold boot - it gets
caught in a loop trying to return from that bios function.  However, if you
start the emulator without the cart, hot insert the cart, and then reset it,
it should run.

I'm wondering how this worked on the real thing.

Next, I'm looking at the graphics glitches in Cosmic Raiders.  I know this
was working originally, and it broke sometime ago, prior to release 0.70.

I'll keep y'all posted...

I've been trying to figure out exactly what tapes have already been
archived, specifically to identify the most needed of the tapes from
atari2600.com, and it's been a little more complicated that I
expected.

Now, of course many tape programs are available on ballyalley.com, and
they're all reasonably well organized.  Sometimes, the source code of
a program is available when an audio file is not, but that's no big
deal--I figure having the source code preserves all the essential
information.

But, things started to get more complicated when I looked at the files
in the Yahoo group and found five large sets of programs, many of
which are unavailable elsewhere.  But fortunately the group has all
its messages archived, so I was able to figure out where they came
from, and eventually realized that even more programs may be archived
already.

It all starts with message #1343.  Somehow, contact was made with Mike
White (author of many Astrocade programming tutorials), who provided a
huge list of software that he had (though the list seems to leave out
some things he eventually provided, such as Whiz Quiz).  Before too
long, he started providing tapes to archive.  Lance got a tape with
something like 100 different programs on it (#1604), saved it as a
.wav file and put the raw recordings online (#1605, 1606).  Along with
the tape, Lance also received a letter from Mike (#1667) and a program
listing (#1672, 1673).  Adam processed most of these files with
ballybin, and in January 2004 uploaded the results in the sets I just
recently came across (#1630, 1634, 1635, 1637, 1662).  A few of the
files he had trouble with, and they weren't included in the sets.  OK,
so far so good.  Lots of new programs have been archived (though not
on ballyalley.com), and the recordings of the troublesome ones are
still online at Lance's own site.

Then, things start to get confusing.  Mike started sending tapes to
Adam instead of Lance (#1729).  Adam archived a bunch of programs, but
said he's waiting to sort everything before putting them online
(#1738).  Adam received still more tapes, including many 300 baud
programs (#1769).  Adam archived some of the 300 baud programs,
including the Bally Program Sampler that I just recently archived and
Lance put on ballyalley.com (#1878).  By this point, Adam was posting
much less frequently, and eventually he seemed to disappear entirely.

So, what happened to all these programs Adam received?  He might have
put some of them on ballyalley.com, but obviously not all of them
since the Bally Program Sampler only recently went up.  Additionally,
some of the programs mentioned in Mike's original list (Road Toad and
Horrible Harry for example) still don't seem to be available.  I'm
still interested in the atari2600.com tapes, of course, but following
up on this might be even more fruitful.

on the tape is exactly the same as the one on the web,

file actually loaded correctly, but when it was
cleaned it showed the title animation, but then
crashed loading the actual game.  I realized that the
problem was that ballybin was inserting only about a
second of silence between the loads, so the second
load (containing the game) would start playing while
the title animation was still processing.  I added
about 13 seconds of silence between the loads,
matching the original, and it worked great.  An
unfortunate side effect is that, while adding the
silence made the .wav file only slightly larger, it
now only gets an 85% compression ratio in .zip format,
while most files get 98%.  I'm not sure why that is.

and the improved version of 3D Tic-Tac-Toe to worry
about on this tape (list part 1).  Lists part 2 and 3,

Castle Bally - Review by Adam Trionfo

It's August 2005 and I just played a new game for the Bally Astrocade.  It's by Paul Pank and it is called "Castle Bally."  This game was written in 2005 (or was it 2004?); this is the first new game for the Bally in a LONG time.

General comments:

1)  When I first played I went South three times and won the game by killing Mordimar.  It took about a minute.  After playing the game more, and looking at the program listing I think that there is supposed to be a battle.  I guess that part isn't finished or didn't work.

2) I explored the game after "beating" it.  I found the Sword of Fire to kill the werewolf (not that he presented a danger; the poor beast just was hanging out there, not even bothering me at all).

3) I found the Shield of Ang by the pond, which I presume would have protected me from Mordimar, but it seemed I killed that evil guy automatically on the first play through.

4) I listed the program and found these four phrases were not used (they're all for the "Battle" with Mordimar, I presume): "Mordimar attacks you!", "The shield blocks him.",  "He attacked you!" and "He missed you"

5) I would suggest the joystick interface that was used in "Cavern Quest" for any possible new version of "Castle Bally," as the Go menu interface is quite annoying- you have to choose GO, and then choose a direction by number.  Since the Bally prints text slowly, this really removes the player from the game.

Comments on language representation:

1) Werewolf is not spelled "Wherewolf"

2) "Slash it dies." should be "Slash, it dies!" or "Slash!  It dies!"

This game is VERY small.  Here are all the room locations, what's in them and what happens when you use the items.

1) You are inside a small church, by an altar [Does this room have a purpose?]
2) You are by the Village near a well (Coil of Rope)
3) You are standing in a forest (Fiery Werewolf) [Use Sword: "Slash, it dies!"]
4) You are in a long hallway [A hallway BEFORE the castle?]
5) You are in a castle by a thrown (Mordimar) [You killed Mordimar.  You've Won!]
6) You are in a valley near a pond (Shield of Ang)
7) You are facing a large oak tree
8) You are upon a branch above the trees (Sword of Fire)

Overall, this is an interesting programming example for a text adventure, but it is FAR from a game.  The 1983 "Cavern Quest" by Bruce Jaeger has FAR more rooms, and it was random- it could be played over again without repetition; that game packed a much more powerful punch.  "Castle Bally" would only hold the attention of someone who might want to try a new game on the Astrocade just for the heck of it and not care WHAT it is.

If you're into text adventures why not try a pass through the classic adventure Zork? The Zork trilogy is free and can be downloaded here:

http://www.csd.uwo.ca/Infocom/download.html

Actually, it's QUITE user friendly, there's hardly any steps at all.  Maybe it seems convoluted because Lance explains how to do it for more than one BASIC?  Though, remember, the target audiance for both the Viper and the Blue Ram Interface were programmers, NOT casual users.  Those were the people that wanted more memory.  Other owners of Astrocades were happy to use the various carts, and when they got tired of the Astrocade they moved onto other systems that had other games.

When the RAM expansion units were released a third party cartridge for the Astrocade had not yet been released (no, not even ONE).  Indeed AstroBASIC had not even been released yet.  There was just the trusty 300 baud BASIC-- that's IT.  It is that interface that all of the other released programming languages use (BASIC and machine language) to load programs.  It would take about EIGHT minutes to load Vipersoft BASIC at 300 baud!  People in the Astrocade community were used to this because there was NOTHING ELSE available and things had ALWAYS been this way.  Sure, they lusted for more, but they took what they could get and what they got was quite powerful.

I'm going to go repeat Lance's instructions because they are perfect, but I'm going to trim them down just for AstroBASIC, hoping to make them less convoluted, and thus make it understood that this process IS user friendly, and it isn't at all a lengthy process.  Anyone who had known how to load a program from tape would have had NO problems with this process.

To Load an Expanded BASIC using the AstroBASIC Interface:

1) Set the RAM protection off.  This will Write Protect RAM set aside for BASIC [or anything you want to load into the cartridge area])

2) Enter this command into BASIC:  &(192)=0;:input %(24576)  [GO]

3) Once BASIC finishes loading, switch the RAM Protection on.  This prevents BASIC from
getting erased during Reset or bad POKE command)

4) To start BASIC, type: CALL 24576 [This starts the program in the cartridge area-- you can also just press Reset].

Not so bad, is it>

Adam

I think you misunderstood what I did.  I had several
300 baud tapes from L&M, all of which ended with
sounds for a ":RETURN; RUN" command.  With most of the
tapes I could record into a computer and get a .wav
file that loaded perfectly into the Astrocade through
the 300 baud interface and ran automatically.  With a
few, however, I could only get a good load directly
into the Astrocade or I had to repair a few characters
that wouldn't load correctly.  Then, to get a .wav
file, I recorded from the Astrocade itself using
":PRINT; LIST".  But these recordings differed from
the original in that they didn't have the ":RETURN;
RUN" command at the end.  To get around this, I used
an audio editing program (Audacity) to copy the end of
one of the good 300 baud .wav files recorded from a
tape onto the end of one of the .wav files recorded
from the Astrocade, thus adding the ":RETURN; RUN"
command and restoring the autorun feature of the
original.  While we do have 2000 baud versions of a
few of these programs (not most), I never had to use
any sounds or code from these.

Paul
